passages.passageHtml:
A comprehensive and satisfied perception of these advantages was uppermost in the minds of this local audience, as they waited for the Bishop to begin his reading. They had entertained this Bishop and his Presiding Elders, and the rank and file of common preachers, in a style which could not have been remotely approached by any other congregation in the Conference. Where else, one would like to know, could the Bishop have been domiciled in a Methodist house where he might have a sitting-room all to himself, with his bedroom leading out of it? Every clergyman present had been provided for in a private residence—even down to the Licensed Exhorters, who were not really ministers at all when you came to think of it, and who might well thank their stars that the Conference had assembled among such open-handed people. There existed a dim feeling that these Licensed Exhorters—an uncouth crew, with country store-keepers and lumbermen and even a horse-doctor among their number—had taken rather too much for granted, and were not exhibiting quite the proper degree of gratitude over their reception.

But a more important issue hung now imminent in the balance—was Tecumseh to be fairly and honorably rewarded for her hospitality by being given the pastor of her choice?

All were agreed—at least among those who paid pew-rents—upon the great importance of a change in the pulpit of the First M. E. Church. A change in persons must of course take place, for their present pastor had exhausted the three-year maximum of the itinerant system, but there was needed much more than that. For a handsome and expensive church building like this, and with such a modern and go-ahead congregation, it was simply a vital necessity to secure an attractive and fashionable preacher. They had held their own against the Presbyterians these past few years only by the most strenuous efforts, and under the depressing disadvantage of a minister who preached dreary out-of-date sermons, and who lacked even the most rudimentary sense of social distinctions. The Presbyterians had captured the new cashier of the Adams County Bank, who had always gone to the Methodist Church in the town he came from, but now was lost solely because of this tiresome old fossil of theirs; and there were numerous other instances of the same sort, scarcely less grievous. That this state of things must be altered was clear.

I call our world Flatland, not because we call it so, but to make its nature clearer to you, my happy readers, who are privileged to live in Space.

Imagine a vast sheet of paper on which straight Lines, Triangles, Squares, Pentagons, Hexagons, and other figures, instead of remaining fixed in their places, move freely about, on or in the surface, but without the power of rising above or sinking below it, very much like shadows—only hard and with luminous edges—and you will then have a pretty correct notion of my country and countrymen. Alas, a few years ago, I should have said "my universe": but now my mind has been opened to higher views of things.

In such a country, you will perceive at once that it is impossible that there should be anything of what you call a "solid" kind; but I dare say you will suppose that we could at least distinguish by sight the Triangles, Squares, and other figures, moving about as I have described them. On the contrary, we could see nothing of the kind, not at least so as to distinguish one figure from another. Nothing was visible, nor could be visible, to us, except Straight Lines; and the necessity of this I will speedily demonstrate.

Place a penny on the middle of one of your tables in Space; and leaning over it, look down upon it. It will appear a circle. But now, drawing back to the edge of the table, gradually lower your eye (thus bringing yourself more and more into the condition of the inhabitants of Flatland), and you will find the penny becoming more and more oval to your view, and at last when you have placed your eye exactly on the edge of the table (so that you are, as it were, actually a Flatlander) the penny will then have ceased to appear oval at all, and will have become, so far as you can see, a straight line.

The same thing would happen if you were to treat in the same way a Triangle, or Square, or any other figure cut out of pasteboard. As soon as you look at it with your eye on the edge on the table, you will find that it ceases to appear to you a figure, and that it becomes in appearance a straight line. Take for example an equilateral Triangle—who represents with us a Tradesman of the respectable class. Fig. 1 represents the Tradesman as you would see him while you were bending over him from above; figs. 2 and 3 represent the Tradesman, as you would see him if your eye were close to the level, or all but on the level of the table; and if your eye were quite on the level of the table (and that is how we see him in Flatland) you would see nothing but a straight line.

When I was in Spaceland I heard that your sailors have very similar experiences while they traverse your seas and discern some distant island or coast lying on the horizon. The far-off land may have bays, forelands, angles in and out to any number and extent; yet at a distance you see none of these (unless indeed your sun shines bright upon them revealing the projections and retirements by means of light and shade), nothing but a grey unbroken line upon the water.

Well, that is just what we see when one of our triangular or other acquaintances comes toward us in Flatland. As there is neither sun with us, nor any light of such a kind as to make shadows, we have none of the helps to the sight that you have in Spaceland. If our friend comes closer to us we see his line becomes larger; if he leaves us it becomes smaller: but still he looks like a straight line; be he a Triangle, Square, Pentagon, Hexagon, Circle, what you will—a straight Line he looks and nothing else.

Some such trite reflection—as apposite to the subject as most random reflections are—passed through the mind of a young man who came out of the front door of the Patesville Hotel about nine o'clock one fine morning in spring, a few years after the Civil War, and started down Front Street toward the market- house. Arriving at the town late the previous evening, he had been driven up from the steamboat in a carriage, from which he had been able to distinguish only the shadowy outlines of the houses along the street; so that this morning walk was his first opportunity to see the town by daylight. ... He saw little that was not familiar, or that he had not seen in his dreams a hundred times during the past ten years. There had been some changes, it is true, some melancholy changes, but scarcely anything by way of addition or improvement to counterbalance them. Here and there blackened and dismantled walls marked the place where handsome buildings once had stood, for Sherman's march to the sea had left its mark upon the town. The stores were mostly of brick, two stories high, joining one another after the manner of cities. Some of the names on the signs were familiar; others, including a number of Jewish names, were quite unknown to him.

A two minutes' walk brought Warwick—the name he had registered under, and as we shall call him —to the market- house, the central feature of Patesville, from both the commercial and the picturesque points of view. ... Warwick was unable to perceive much change in the market- house. Perhaps the surface of the red brick, long unpainted, had scaled off a little more here and there. There might have been a slight accretion of the moss and lichen on the shingled roof. But the tall tower, with its four- faced clock, rose as majestically and uncompromisingly as though the land had never been subjugated. Was it so irreconcilable, Warwick wondered, as still to peal out the curfew bell, which at nine o'clock at night had clamorously warned all negroes, slave or free, that it was unlawful for them to be abroad after that hour, under penalty of imprisonment or whipping? ... A few moments later, Warwick saw a colored policeman in the old constable's place—a stronger reminder than even the burned buildings that war had left its mark upon the old town, with which Time had dealt so tenderly.

... He threw a glance toward a certain corner where steps led to the town hall above. On this stairway he had once seen a manacled free negro shot while being taken upstairs for examination under a criminal charge. Warwick recalled vividly how the shot had rung out. He could see again the livid look of terror on the victim's face, the gathering crowd, the resulting confusion. The murderer, he recalled, had been tried and sentenced to imprisonment for life, but was pardoned by a merciful governor after serving a year of his sentence. As Warwick was neither a prophet nor the son of a prophet, he could not foresee that, thirty years later, even this would seem an excessive punishment for so slight a misdemeanor.

The next day my mother and Rose hastened to pay their compliments to the fair recluse; and came back but little wiser than they went; though my mother declared she did not regret the journey, for if she had not gained much good, she flattered herself she had imparted some, and that was better: she had given some useful advice, which, she hoped, would not be thrown away; for Mrs. Graham, though she said little to any purpose, and appeared somewhat self-opinionated, seemed not incapable of reflection, though she did not know where she had been all her life, poor thing, for she betrayed a lamentable ignorance on certain points, and had not even the sense to be ashamed of it.

"On what points, mother?" asked I.

"On household matters, and all the little niceties of cookery, and such things, that every lady ought to be familiar with, whether she be required to make a practical use of her knowledge or not. I gave her some useful pieces of information, however, and several excellent receipts, the value of which she evidently could not appreciate, for she begged I would not trouble myself, as she lived in such a plain, quiet way, that she was sure she should never make use of them. 'No matter, my dear,' said I; 'it is what every respectable female ought to know;—and besides, though you are alone now, you will not be always so; you have been married, and probably—I might say almost certainly—will be again.' 'You are mistaken there, ma'am,' said she, almost haughtily; 'I am certain I never shall.'—But I told her I knew better."

"Some romantic young widow, I suppose," said I, "come there to end her days in solitude, and mourn in secret for the dear departed—but it won't last long."

"No, I think not," observed Rose; "for she didn't seem very disconsolate after all; and she's excessively pretty—handsome rather—you must see her, Gilbert; you will call her a perfect beauty..."

The next day was Saturday; and, on Sunday, everybody wondered whether or not the fair unknown would profit by the vicar's remonstrance, and come to church. I confess I looked with some interest myself towards the old family pew, appertaining to Wildfell Hall...

And there I beheld a tall, lady-like figure, clad in black. Her face was towards me, and there was something in it which, once seen, invited me to look again. Her hair was raven black, and disposed in long glossy ringlets... her complexion was clear and pale... the brows above were expressive and well defined; the forehead was lofty and intellectual, the nose a perfect aquiline and the features, in general, unexceptionable—only there was a slight hollowness about the cheeks and eyes, and the lips, though finely formed, were a little too thin, a little too firmly compressed, and had something about them that betokened, I thought, no very soft or amiable temper; and I said in my heart—"I would rather admire you from this distance, fair lady, than be the partner of your home."

Just then she happened to raise her eyes, and they met mine; I did not choose to withdraw my gaze, and she turned again to her book, but with a momentary, indefinable expression of quiet scorn, that was inexpressibly provoking to me.

By the first week in September I had abandoned all palliatives, and had settled into the dismal but dignified routine of office, club, and chambers. And now came the most cruel trial, for the hideous truth dawned on me that the world I found so indispensable could after all dispense with me. It was all very well for Lady Ashleigh to assure me that I was deeply missed; but a letter from F—, who was one of the party, written "in haste, just starting to shoot", and coming as a tardy reply to one of my cleverest, made me aware that the house party had suffered little from my absence. A thrust which smarted more came from my cousin Nesta, who wrote: "It's horrid for you to have to be baking in London now; but, after all, it must be a great pleasure to you to have such interesting and important work to do." Here was a nemesis for an innocent illusion I had been accustomed to foster in the minds of my relations. For the plain truth was that my work was neither interesting nor important, and consisted chiefly at present in smoking cigarettes, in saying that Mr So-and-So was away, in being absent for lunch from twelve till two, and in my spare moments making precis of consular reports.

Only one thing was needed to fill my cup of bitterness, and this it was that specially occupied me as I dressed for dinner this evening. Two days more in this dead and fermenting city and my slavery would be at an end. Yes, but—irony of ironies!—I had nowhere to go to! Invitations for a later date, which I had declined in July with a gratifying sense of being much in request, now rose up spectrally to taunt me. There was at least one which I could easily have revived, but neither in this case nor in any other had there been any renewal of pressure, and there are moments when the difference between proposing oneself and surrendering as a prize to one of several eagerly competing hostesses seems too crushing to be contemplated. In short, I was at the extremity of depression.

The usual scuffle on the staircase prepared me for the entry of Withers, who handed me a letter bearing a German postmark. A momentary thrill of curiosity broke in upon my depression as I sat down to open it. The letter was from an old Oxford acquaintance, Arthur H. Davies, whom I had not seen regularly in years. He invited me to join him on a yachting trip in the Baltic for duck-shooting. I crumpled the letter into my pocket and started languidly for my club. The dinner was execrable, the ventilation a farce. And yet I was puzzled to find that somewhere within me there was a faint lightening of the spirits. Could it be Davies's letter? Yachting in the Baltic at the end of September! The very idea made one shudder. Every sane yachtsman was paying off his crew now. Why a prismatic compass? I pulled out the letter again, and ran down its impulsive sentences, affecting to ignore what a gust of fresh air, high spirits, and good fellowship this flimsy bit of paper wafted into the jaded clubroom.

questions.questionHtml: Which of the following best captures the main idea of this excerpt?

options.A: The congregation of Tecumseh is deeply religious and believes that hosting the Conference will bring them spiritual rewards.
options.B: The congregation's pride in their hospitality is matched by their desire to gain a fashionable preacher to improve their social standing.
options.C: The Bishop and Presiding Elders were treated better in Tecumseh than anywhere else, but the Licensed Exhorters failed to show proper gratitude.
options.D: The competition with Presbyterians has forced the Methodist congregation to focus on money and appearance rather than faith.

questions.explanationHtml:
Explanation of each option:

Why B is correct: The passage opens with the congregation's "comprehensive and satisfied perception" of their own hospitality, then immediately frames the "more important issue" as whether they will be "rewarded" with the pastor they want. Their desire for a "fashionable preacher" is explicitly tied to competing with Presbyterians, not to spiritual concerns. The main idea combines pride in hospitality with a demand for social reward.

Why A is wrong: Nowhere does the passage say they expect spiritual rewards. Their focus is on social standing, competition, and appearances.

Why C is wrong: This is a minor detail (the Exhorters' ingratitude), not the central argument. The excerpt spends far more time on the pastor selection.

Why D is wrong: The passage shows a priority on social status but never claims that faith has been abandoned or that money/appearance have replaced faith. D overstates and introduces an absolute not supported by the text.

questions.questionHtml: The author mentions that the current pastor "lacked even the most rudimentary sense of social distinctions." How does this detail function in the passage?

options.A: It explains why the pastor's sermons were unpopular with the wealthiest members of the congregation.
options.B: It serves as evidence that the congregation's primary concern is social status rather than spiritual leadership.
options.C: It contrasts with the congregation's own strong awareness of social class, which they expect their pastor to share.
options.D: It shows that the pastor was incompetent in all aspects of his job, including preaching and administration.

questions.explanationHtml:
Explanation of each option:

Why C is correct: The congregation is acutely aware of social distinctions (pew rents, fashionable events, competition with Presbyterians). The pastor's lack of that awareness is a flaw from their point of view. The detail functions as a contrast between the congregation's values and the pastor's, which explains why they want a new preacher who shares their social consciousness.

Why A is wrong: The passage separates the criticism of sermons ("dreary out-of-date") from the criticism of social awareness. It never links the pastor's lack of social distinctions specifically to the wealthiest members or directly to sermon unpopularity.

Why B is wrong: This answer confuses what the detail proves with how it functions. The detail is evidence of their social concern, but its function in the passage is to create a contrast that justifies their desire for a fashionable preacher. B is too direct and misses the rhetorical role.

Why D is wrong: The passage criticizes the pastor's sermons and social sense but never claims incompetence in "all aspects" such as administration, pastoral care, or theology. D is an unsupported overgeneralization.

questions.questionHtml: The claim that Tecumseh's congregation is "modern and go-ahead" is best supported by which detail?

options.A: They have almost entirely abolished free pews and rent the front rows for one hundred dollars each.
options.B: They believe securing an "attractive and fashionable preacher" is a "vital necessity."
options.C: They provided private housing even for Licensed Exhorters, who are not fully ordained ministers.
options.D: They have held their own against the Presbyterians only through "most strenuous efforts."

questions.explanationHtml:
Explanation of each option:

Why B is correct: The phrase "modern and go-ahead" appears in the sentence: "For a handsome and expensive church building like this, and with such a modern and go-ahead congregation, it was simply a vital necessity to secure an attractive and fashionable preacher." The detail that immediately follows and directly supports the claim is their belief that a fashionable preacher is a "vital necessity." This links their modern, progressive identity directly to social competition and image.

Why A is wrong: Abolishing free pews and charging high rents does suggest a modern, businesslike attitude. However, the passage does not explicitly connect this practice to the label "modern and go-ahead." A student might reasonably choose A, but B is more directly supported because the label is immediately followed by the need for a fashionable preacher. A is a good distractor because it's partially correct but not the best evidence.

Why C is wrong: Providing housing for Exhorters shows generosity, which could be traditional Christian hospitality, not necessarily "modern" or "go-ahead." It does not signal progressiveness or social ambition.

Why D is wrong: Struggling to hold their own against Presbyterians is a problem they face, not evidence of being modern and go-ahead. In fact, it shows they are currently at a disadvantage.

questions.questionHtml: Which detail from the excerpt most clearly reveals the congregation's underlying belief that social image matters more than religious substance?

options.A: "They had held their own against the Presbyterians these past few years only by the most strenuous efforts"
options.B: "the Presbyterians had captured the new cashier of the Adams County Bank ... who had always gone to the Methodist Church"
options.C: "it was simply a vital necessity to secure an attractive and fashionable preacher"
options.D: "Every clergyman present had been provided for in a private residence—even down to the Licensed Exhorters"

questions.explanationHtml:
Explanation of each option:

Why C is correct: Calling an attractive, fashionable preacher a "vital necessity" for a church building and congregation directly places social appeal (fashion, attractiveness) above any spiritual qualification (piety, biblical knowledge, preaching ability). This most clearly reveals that social image is their true priority.

Why A is wrong: Holding their own against Presbyterians could be about numbers, budget, or institutional survival, not necessarily social image over faith. It is ambiguous and does not explicitly elevate style over substance.

Why B is wrong: Losing the cashier is a consequence of the pastor's lack of social distinctions. The detail itself reports a loss, not the congregation's value judgment. While it supports the theme indirectly, it does not clearly reveal the belief that image matters more than faith. C is the direct expression of that belief.

Why D is wrong: Providing housing for all clergy, including lowly Exhorters, could be interpreted as Christian charity or humility, not social climbing. It does not clearly show misplaced priorities.

questions.questionHtml: The author includes the description of a penny on a table primarily to:

options.A: Prove that Flatlanders are mistaken when they believe they see only straight lines
options.B: Provide a step-by-step demonstration that a three-dimensional object can appear as a straight line when viewed from a limited perspective
options.C: Contrast the way round objects appear in Spaceland versus the way triangular objects appear in Flatland
options.D: Suggest that Spacelanders would have the same difficulty as Flatlanders if they lowered their eyes to table level

questions.explanationHtml:
Explanation of all options:

A is incorrect. The author uses the penny to confirm that Flatlanders see only straight lines, not to prove them mistaken. The penny experiment shows exactly what Flatlanders experience. This option misunderstands the author's purpose.

B is correct. The author guides the reader through lowering their eye from above to table level, showing the penny changing from circle to oval to straight line. This step-by-step demonstration proves that from a Flatlander's edge-on perspective, even a round object appears as a line. The purpose is to demonstrate the geometric principle behind the main idea.

C is incorrect. The author is not contrasting round objects with triangular objects. He uses a penny (round) as an example, then explicitly says the same thing happens with a triangle or square. The focus is on all shapes, not a contrast between types.

D is incorrect. While it is true that a Spacelander at table level would see a line, that is not the primary purpose of the penny example. The primary purpose is to demonstrate why Flatlanders see lines, not to draw a comparison about Spacelanders' difficulties. This option confuses an implication with the main purpose.

questions.questionHtml: Which detail from the passage most directly supports the main idea that a Flatlander cannot visually distinguish one type of shape from another?

options.A: "Fig. 1 represents the Tradesman as you would see him while you were bending over him from above"
options.B: "The far-off land may have bays, forelands, angles in and out to any number and extent; yet at a distance you see none of these"
options.C: "If our friend comes closer to us we see his line becomes larger; if he leaves us it becomes smaller: but still he looks like a straight line"
options.D: "As there is neither sun with us, nor any light of such a kind as to make shadows, we have none of the helps to the sight that you have"

questions.explanationHtml:
Explanation of all options:

A is incorrect. This detail describes how a Tradesman (triangle) appears when viewed from above (Fig. 1). That is the Spacelander's perspective, not the Flatlander's. It actually shows that shapes can be distinguished from above, which is the opposite of the main idea about Flatland.

B is incorrect. This is the sailor-coastline analogy from Spaceland. While it illustrates the general concept of reduced perception at a distance, it does not directly describe what Flatlanders see of each other. It is an analogy, not direct evidence about Flatland figures.

C is correct. This sentence directly states that no matter what shape the Flatlander's acquaintance is (Triangle, Square, Pentagon, Hexagon, Circle), it "still looks like a straight line." Even as size changes, the appearance remains a line with no distinguishing features. This is the most direct support for the main idea that shapes cannot be told apart by sight.

D is incorrect. This detail explains the cause of the visual limitation (no sun, no shadows). It supports a different claim—why Flatlanders cannot see shapes—but not the main idea that they actually cannot distinguish them. The main idea is the fact of indistinguishability; this option addresses the reason behind it.

questions.questionHtml: A student claims: "The author uses the sailor-coastline analogy to prove that Flatlanders are actually better off than Spacelanders because they don't need sunlight to see." How does the passage address this claim?

options.A: It directly supports the claim by stating that sailors see only a grey unbroken line, just like Flatlanders
options.B: It contradicts the claim by explaining that Spacelanders have sunlight which can reveal details, while Flatlanders have no such advantage
options.C: It neither supports nor contradicts the claim because the analogy focuses only on distance, not on quality of vision
options.D: It supports the claim indirectly by showing that both sailors and Flatlanders see only lines, making their situations identical

questions.explanationHtml:
Explanation of all options:

A is incorrect. The passage does state that sailors see a "grey unbroken line," just as Flatlanders do. However, this similarity does not mean Flatlanders are "better off." The passage immediately notes that sailors could see details if sunlight revealed them, while Flatlanders have no such help. This option ignores the key difference and therefore misrepresents the passage.

B is correct. The passage directly contradicts the student's claim. It explains that Spacelanders have sunlight, which "reveals the projections and retirements" of a coastline, giving them an advantage. Flatlanders have "neither sun nor any light of such a kind as to make shadows," so they lack that help. Thus, Flatlanders are worse off, not better.

C is incorrect. The passage does not remain neutral. It explicitly contrasts the presence of sunlight in Spaceland with its absence in Flatland. The analogy is used to highlight a difference, not to avoid the issue. This option incorrectly claims the passage takes no position.

D is incorrect. The situations are not identical. Sailors may see only a line at a distance, but they have the potential to see details with sunlight. Flatlanders never have that potential. The passage directly states this difference, so it does not support the claim that their situations are identical.

questions.questionHtml: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's argument that Flatlanders can see "nothing... except Straight Lines"?

options.A: Evidence that some Flatlanders have trained themselves to detect slight differences in line brightness caused by different angles of edges
options.B: Proof that the penny experiment only works with circular objects, not with polygons
options.C: A statement from the author admitting that his mind "has been opened to higher views" after visiting Spaceland
options.D: A demonstration that when a Triangle moves very quickly, its appearance changes from a line to a blurry shape

questions.explanationHtml:
Explanation of all options:

A is correct. The author argues that Flatlanders see "nothing... except Straight Lines" with no way to distinguish shapes. If Flatlanders could detect differences in line brightness caused by different edge angles, that would provide a way to tell shapes apart (e.g., a triangle's edges might produce a different brightness pattern than a square's). This would directly weaken the absolute claim that they see "nothing except" lines without any distinguishing features.

B is incorrect. While this would show a flaw in the penny example, the author explicitly says "the same thing would happen" with triangles and squares. Even if the penny experiment failed for polygons, the author could still rely on the triangle/square examples. Weakening one piece of evidence does not destroy the overall argument, especially since the claim is supported by multiple examples.

C is incorrect. The author's comment about his mind being "opened to higher views" refers to understanding the existence of multiple dimensions (Spaceland). It has nothing to do with the visual limitation of seeing only straight lines in Flatland. This statement is irrelevant to the argument about perception.

D is incorrect. Seeing a "blurry shape" instead of a straight line does not help a Flatlander distinguish one shape from another. A blurry triangle and a blurry square would still look the same—indistinguishable. Moreover, the author describes normal movement ("comes toward us"), not high speed. This option does not provide a way to tell shapes apart, so it does not weaken the claim.

questions.questionHtml: Which of the following statements best expresses the main idea of the passage, as supported by specific details?

options.A: The physical destruction caused by Sherman's march is the most significant change in Patesville, because the passage describes burned buildings before anything else.
options.B: The town has experienced only superficial physical decay, but the deeper changes involve who holds authority and how racial control is enforced.
options.C: Warwick is disappointed that the town has not progressed economically, as shown by the lack of new stores and the presence of unfamiliar Jewish names.
options.D: The market-house remains a symbol of unchanging Southern pride, and the colored policeman is merely a minor adjustment to an otherwise intact social order.

questions.explanationHtml:
Explanation of each option:

Option A is incorrect. Although the passage does mention burned buildings from Sherman's march, it immediately downplays their significance by saying there were "scarcely anything by way of addition or improvement to counterbalance them" and then later calls the colored policeman a "stronger reminder" of the war's mark. The main idea is not simply physical destruction; the passage explicitly ranks the policeman as more important than the burned walls.

Option B is correct. The passage repeatedly notes that physical structures (like the market-house) have changed very little ("unable to perceive much change"). Yet the presence of a "colored policeman" replacing the old constable who enforced the racist curfew is highlighted as a profound social change. The question about whether the curfew bell still rings also points to a shift in racial enforcement. Thus, the main idea is that deep changes are in authority and racial control, not in buildings.

Option C is incorrect. The mention of Jewish names on store signs is a brief, minor observation. Nowhere does the passage state that Warwick cares about economic progress or that the lack of new stores disappoints him. This option misreads a small detail as the central theme.

Option D is incorrect. While the market-house does appear "uncompromising," the narrator explicitly says the colored policeman is a stronger reminder of the war's impact, not a minor adjustment. The social order has changed in a meaningful way, even if the building looks the same.

questions.questionHtml: The author includes the anecdote about a free negro being shot on the stairway and the murderer being pardoned after one year. This evidence most directly supports which of the following claims?

options.A: In the pre-war South, white violence against Black people was rarely punished severely, and even when a sentence was given, it was often reduced.
options.B: Warwick personally witnessed this event, which proves that he is a former resident of Patesville with deep emotional scars from the past.
options.C: The legal system in the South became much harsher after the war, because the narrator contrasts the pardon with the later "excessive punishment."
options.D: Shooting a manacled prisoner was considered a minor crime, since the governor pardoned the murderer after only one year in prison.

questions.explanationHtml:
Explanation of each option:

Option A is correct. The anecdote shows that a white man who shot a manacled free negro received a life sentence but was pardoned after only one year. This indicates that even when a harsh sentence was given, it was quickly reduced. The final sentence adds that thirty years later people would see the punishment (the one-year pardon) as excessive for a "slight misdemeanor" – implying that the shooting itself was treated leniently by the standards of the time. This directly supports the claim that anti-Black violence was not severely punished.

Option B is incorrect. While Warwick "recalled" the event, the passage does not state that he personally witnessed it (he "had once seen" could mean he saw it, but that is not the point). More importantly, the purpose of the anecdote is not to prove Warwick's residency or emotional state; it is to illustrate a moral and legal standard. The question asks what claim the evidence directly supports, and B focuses on Warwick's personal history rather than the broader social claim.

Option C is incorrect. The phrase "excessive punishment" refers to the life sentence commuted to one year, not to a later harsher system. The narrator says "even this" (the one-year pardon) would seem excessive. There is no comparison showing the post-war system as harsher. This option misinterprets the temporal contrast.

Option D is incorrect. The governor's pardon does not prove that the act was legally considered a minor crime. The murderer was initially sentenced to life imprisonment, which shows the act was taken seriously. The pardon reflects mercy or racial bias, not the legal classification of the offense. The final sentence is the author's ironic commentary, not a statement of contemporary law.

questions.questionHtml: The passage contains a potential tension: the narrator says the colored policeman is "a stronger reminder than even the burned buildings that war had left its mark." How does the detail about the curfew bell (which warned negroes not to be abroad at night) function in relation to this statement?

options.A: The curfew bell supports the idea by showing that one system of racial control (a bell enforced by a white constable) has been replaced by a different system (a Black policeman), highlighting both change and continuity.
options.B: The curfew bell contradicts the idea because if the bell still rings, then nothing has really changed; the policeman would just be a Black face doing the same white-supremacist work.
options.C: The curfew bell is irrelevant to the idea; it merely describes the physical features of the market- house tower and has no connection to social or racial change.
options.D: The curfew bell weakens the idea by suggesting that the bell itself is a more powerful symbol of oppression than any person in uniform could ever be.

questions.explanationHtml:
Explanation of each option:

Option A is correct. The curfew bell represents the old system of racial control (white-enforced restriction on Black movement). Warwick wonders if it still rings. The presence of a colored policeman in the old constable's place suggests a new figure of authority. The bell detail supports the idea that war left a mark not by erasing racial control but by changing who enforces it. This creates the tension of change within continuity, which makes the policeman a stronger reminder.

Option B is incorrect. While this is a plausible critical reading, the passage does not present the bell as contradicting the narrator's statement. The narrator explicitly says the policeman is a stronger reminder than burned buildings. If the bell still rings, that would actually deepen the irony, but the passage does not use the bell to argue that nothing changed. Option B rejects the narrator's own ranking without textual support.

Option C is incorrect. The curfew bell is directly linked to racial laws ("clamorously warned all negroes ... it was unlawful for them to be abroad"). It is not a neutral physical detail; it carries strong social meaning.

Option D is incorrect. The passage does not compare the bell's power to a person's. The bell is mentioned separately, and the narrator's contrast is between the policeman and burned buildings, not between the policeman and the bell. This option invents a comparison the text does not make.

questions.questionHtml: Based on the evidence in the passage, which of the following best summarizes Warwick's perspective on the town of Patesville?

options.A: Warwick is a detached stranger who sees the town's changes as a natural, unemotional process of aging and decay, with no personal connection.
options.B: Warwick is a former resident who recognizes nearly everything but views the post-war changes as mostly negative, superficial, or bittersweet.
options.C: Warwick is an enthusiastic supporter of Reconstruction who celebrates the colored policeman as a sign of full racial equality and progress.
options.D: Warwick is a disillusioned Northerner who expected the town to be completely rebuilt but finds only ruins and unfamiliar names.

questions.explanationHtml:
Explanation of each option:

Option A is incorrect. Although the opening calls his reflection "trite," the rest of the passage shows emotional language: he sees "melancholy changes," wonders if the "irreconcilable" clock tower still rings the racist curfew, and feels "affection and bitterness" (from the full text, but even in this excerpt, his reaction is not detached). He also recognizes the town as familiar, not as a stranger.

Option B is correct. Warwick "saw little that was not familiar," indicating he knows the town from before. He calls the changes "melancholy" and notes there is "scarcely anything ... to counterbalance them." His question about the curfew bell ("Was it so irreconcilable...?") suggests a bitter, affectionate, and somewhat sad perspective. This matches a former resident who finds the post-war changes mostly negative or bittersweet.

Option C is incorrect. There is no evidence that Warwick celebrates the colored policeman. The narrator calls it a "reminder" of war's mark, not a sign of progress or equality. Warwick's tone is not enthusiastic; he seems troubled by the changes.

Option D is incorrect. Warwick is from South Carolina (the register says "Clarence, South Carolina"), not a Northerner. He finds things familiar, not completely ruined or alien. He does not express disappointment that the town wasn't rebuilt; he notes the lack of improvement but also recognizes the old structures.

questions.questionHtml: Which detail from the passage most directly undermines the narrator's mother's belief that she has successfully "imparted some good" to Mrs. Graham?

options.A: Mrs. Graham lived "in such a plain, quiet way" that she would never use recipes.
options.B: Mrs. Graham told the mother she was "certain" she would never marry again.
options.C: Mrs. Graham appeared "self-opinionated" but "not incapable of reflection."
options.D: Mrs. Graham did not attend church the previous Sunday, despite the vicar's concern.

questions.explanationHtml:
Explanation of why A is correct:

The mother believes she "imparted some good" - meaning she gave useful advice that Mrs. Graham will benefit from. The detail in A shows Mrs. Graham explicitly stating she will never use those recipes because she lives a "plain, quiet way." This directly contradicts the mother's belief that her advice was valuable or welcomed. It undermines the idea that any "good" was successfully imparted.

Explanation of option B (incorrect):

Mrs. Graham's refusal to agree that she will marry again does show she resists the mother's opinion, but the mother's claim of "imparting some good" refers specifically to the household advice and recipes she gave. The remarriage comment is a separate prediction, not the "good" the mother was talking about. Choosing B would confuse two different topics.

Explanation of option C (incorrect):

This detail is actually the mother's own observation. She says Mrs. Graham is "self-opinionated" but "not incapable of reflection." That does not undermine her belief - if anything, it supports her hope that Mrs. Graham might eventually learn. A student might pick this because it sounds like a criticism, but it's not a direct contradiction of "imparted good."

Explanation of option D (incorrect):

Mrs. Graham's absence from church the previous Sunday is unrelated to the mother's visit or the advice she gave. This detail might show Mrs. Graham is unconventional, but it does not address whether the mother's advice was successfully imparted. It is a distractor that shifts the focus to a different event.

questions.questionHtml: Based on the evidence in the passage, what can be most reasonably inferred about why Gilbert says he would "rather admire from this distance than be the partner of your home"?

options.A: He is intimidated by her wealth and social status, which he believes are far above his own.
options.B: He is already emotionally attached to Eliza Millward and feels guilty for looking at another woman.
options.C: He is physically attracted to her but suspects her personality may be cold, proud, or difficult.
options.D: He is angry that she ignored his mother's advice and wants to punish her by keeping his distance.

questions.explanationHtml:
Explanation of why C is correct:

Gilbert describes her as having "unexceptionable" features (meaning nearly perfect) - he is clearly attracted. But he also notices her lips are "too thin, too firmly compressed," which he interprets as indicating "no very soft or amiable temper." Then he says he would rather admire from a distance than be her partner. This shows a combination of attraction and wariness about her personality being cold or proud.

Explanation of option A (incorrect):

Nothing in the passage mentions Mrs. Graham's wealth or social status. Gilbert never expresses intimidation about class differences. This option introduces an idea not supported by the text.

Explanation of option B (incorrect):

Eliza Millward is mentioned earlier in the larger text, but not in this church scene. Gilbert does not reference her, nor does he express guilt. This option asks the reader to bring in outside information that is not present in the given passage.

Explanation of option D (incorrect):

Gilbert never mentions his mother's advice in the church scene. His reaction is based on Mrs. Graham's physical features and her expression of "quiet scorn" when their eyes meet. There is no evidence he is angry about the recipes or household conversation. This option misattributes a motive not found in the text.

questions.questionHtml: A central idea of the passage is that the community misreads or projects onto Mrs. Graham. Which pair of details best supports this idea?

options.A: The mother says Mrs. Graham "had not even the sense to be ashamed" of her ignorance; Gilbert calls her a "romantic young widow."
options.B: Rose says Mrs. Graham is "excessively pretty"; Gilbert notices her "raven black" hair and "aquiline" nose.
options.C: Mrs. Graham rejects the recipes; she also raises her eyes and looks at Gilbert with "quiet scorn."
options.D: The mother claims Mrs. Graham will "probably" marry again; Mrs. Graham says she is "certain" she never shall.

questions.explanationHtml:
Explanation of why A is correct:

The mother misreads Mrs. Graham's lack of domestic knowledge as something shameful ("had not even the sense to be ashamed"). Gilbert misreads her situation by calling her a "romantic young widow" who will eventually remarry. Both are projections - they are not facts about Mrs. Graham but assumptions the community makes. This pair of details directly supports the idea that the community misreads or projects onto her.

Explanation of option B (incorrect):

Rose and Gilbert are simply describing her physical appearance (pretty, raven hair, aquiline nose). These are factual observations, not misreadings or projections. This pair does not support the idea of misreading character.

Explanation of option C (incorrect):

Mrs. Graham's rejection of recipes and her scornful look are her actual actions and expressions. They are not examples of the community misreading her; they are her own behaviors. This option confuses the subject of the central idea.

Explanation of option D (incorrect):

This pair shows a direct disagreement (mother says she will marry again, Mrs. Graham says she will not). While the mother is wrong, this is a single point of factual contradiction, not a pattern of misreading her character or projecting motives. Option A shows two different types of misinterpretation (moral judgment and romantic projection), which better supports the central idea.

questions.questionHtml: Which statement about judging others is most fully supported by both the mother's visit and Gilbert's observations in church?

options.A: First impressions based on physical appearance are usually accurate and should be trusted.
options.B: People often mistake a woman's independence or reserve for ignorance, sadness, or bad temper.
options.C: A person who refuses practical advice from others is inevitably doomed to loneliness and failure.
options.D: Young men are better judges of character than older women because they are less biased by gossip.

questions.explanationHtml:
Explanation of why B is correct:

The mother interprets Mrs. Graham's lack of interest in cookery as "ignorance" and something to be ashamed of - a misreading of her independent choice to live simply. Gilbert interprets her facial features (thin, compressed lips) as a sign of "no very soft or amiable temper" - a misreading of her reserve as coldness. Both are judging her independence or reserve negatively. This supports the theme that people often mistake a woman's autonomy for flaws.

Explanation of option A (incorrect):

The passage actually suggests the opposite. Gilbert's first impression of her face (beautiful but cold) is shown as possibly inaccurate, and he himself admits he is only guessing about her temper. The passage does not endorse trusting first appearances.

Explanation of option C (incorrect):

This statement is extreme and unsupported. Mrs. Graham refuses recipes and lives alone, but the passage says nothing about her being "doomed to loneliness and failure." In fact, she seems content with her plain, quiet life. This option imposes a moral judgment not found in the text.

Explanation of option D (incorrect):

Gilbert is clearly biased - he calls her a "romantic young widow" and assumes she has a bad temper. The mother is also biased, but the passage does not compare them or conclude that young men are better judges. This option introduces a comparison not supported by any evidence in the passage.

questions.questionHtml: The narrator says the "hideous truth" is that the world can dispense with him. Which detail best contradicts the idea that others see him as a self-sacrificing martyr?

options.A: Lady Ashleigh's assurance that he is "deeply missed" at the house party.
options.B: His cousin Nesta's comment that he must take "great pleasure" in having important work.
options.C: The fact that he spends his days smoking cigarettes and making précis of reports.
options.D: F—'s tardy reply, written "in haste, just starting to shoot".

questions.explanationHtml:
Explanation of each option:

A is incorrect but plausible: Lady Ashleigh's assurance seems to support his martyrdom, but the narrator immediately undermines it with evidence that it's empty. A careful reader sees she is just being polite. The question asks for a detail that contradicts the martyr idea – A actually agrees with it on the surface, making it a trap.

B is correct: Nesta's comment is sarcastic. She pretends to believe his work is important, but the sarcasm ("must be a great pleasure") actually exposes that she (and others) see through his martyr act. This directly contradicts the narrator's self-image as a self-sacrificing martyr.

C is incorrect: This detail supports his own claim that his work is boring, but it doesn't show what others think of his martyrdom. It's about his self-awareness, not others' perceptions.

D is incorrect: F—'s tardy reply does show he wasn't missed, which supports the "hideous truth" – but it doesn't specifically contradict the martyr image; it just shows absence of attention. Nesta's sarcasm is more direct and cutting.

questions.questionHtml: The narrator claims he is at "the extremity of depression" primarily because of a social wound, not just boredom. Which detail best supports this specific cause?

options.A: Lady Ashleigh's letter assured him he was "deeply missed" at the party.
options.B: He had declined several invitations in July, and now none have been renewed.
options.C: His work consists of saying "Mr So-and-So is away" and taking long lunch breaks.
options.D: Davies's letter mentions "a prismatic compass" and "Raven mixture".

questions.explanationHtml:
Explanation of each option:

A is incorrect but plausible: Lady Ashleigh saying he is "deeply missed" sounds like social validation, but the narrator has already dismissed it as empty politeness. A student might think this detail supports the idea of a social wound (because it's about social interaction), but in fact it does the opposite – it's a false comfort. The distractor tempts those who don't read carefully.

B is correct: The passage explicitly says the "cup of bitterness" is filled by having "nowhere to go" and that invitations he once proudly declined now "taunt" him with no renewal of pressure. This is a social humiliation – from being "much in request" to being unwanted. That is a social wound, not mere boredom.

C is incorrect: Boring work is frustrating, but the narrator calls it a "plain truth" without linking it directly to the extremity of depression. That extreme comes right after discussing invitations, not work.

D is incorrect: The odd items in Davies's letter are puzzling but not the source of his depression – they come after he already describes being at the extremity. This distractor tests whether the student confuses later events with causes.

questions.questionHtml: Even though the narrator dismisses Davies's yachting offer as foolish ("every sane yachtsman was paying off his crew"), he admits a "faint lightening of the spirits". What is the relationship between the detail about the letter wafting "a gust of fresh air, high spirits, and good fellowship" and this change in mood?

options.A: The detail exaggerates the change, since the narrator still thinks the trip is absurd.
options.B: The detail directly causes the change by providing an emotional contrast to his isolation.
options.C: The detail contradicts the change by reminding him of all the reasons to refuse.
options.D: The detail is irrelevant to the change because the narrator later calls the letter "flimsy".

questions.explanationHtml:
Explanation of each option:

A is incorrect: "Exaggerates" is not accurate – the passage doesn't suggest the change is exaggerated; it's real but unexpected. This distractor tests whether the student confuses "exaggeration" with "genuine but puzzling change."

B is correct: The detail about "a gust of fresh air, high spirits, and good fellowship" is the direct cause of his mood change. The narrator is puzzled because his rational mind rejects the trip, but the emotional tone of the letter lifts his spirits. The relationship is cause-and-effect.

C is incorrect: The detail does not contradict the change – the objections (sane yachtsmen leaving, etc.) are separate thoughts before he pulls the letter out again. The "gust of fresh air" is explicitly positive. This distractor tests whether the student misreads the sequence.

D is incorrect: "Irrelevant" is false – the narrator directly links the letter to his mood. Calling it "flimsy" is a dismissive word, but he still feels the effect. This distractor tests whether the student takes one word out of context.

questions.questionHtml: The narrator lists several objections: "Yachting in the Baltic at the end of September! ... Every sane yachtsman was paying off his crew now. Why a prismatic compass?" What main idea do these objections most directly support when read together with his admission of a "lightening of the spirits"?

options.A: Davies is an incompetent sailor who does not understand safe yachting practices.
options.B: The narrator is genuinely too overworked and important to accept the invitation.
options.C: The Baltic Sea in autumn is objectively dangerous for small yachts.
options.D: The narrator is rationalizing his hesitation while already feeling drawn to the trip.

questions.explanationHtml:
Explanation of each option:

A is incorrect: There is no evidence Davies is incompetent; the narrator simply doesn't understand the equipment. This distractor tempts readers who jump to negative conclusions about the letter's oddness without evidence.

B is incorrect: The narrator explicitly admitted earlier that his work is neither interesting nor important. He is not overworked – he is bored. This distractor tests whether you remember that earlier, easily overlooked detail.

C is incorrect: This is too literal and narrow. Even if the Baltic is dangerous in autumn, the passage is not about Baltic dangers – it's about the narrator's internal conflict. This distractor picks a surface-level fact but misses the main idea of the paragraph.

D is correct: The objections are all logical reasons to refuse, yet the narrator already feels a "lightening of spirits." The best reading is that he is arguing with himself – listing sensible objections to suppress an attraction he already feels. This is rationalization (or internal conflict).
